## 🧩 The mystery

It is your first week in the lab. Prof. Zola drops **300 GB** of sequencing data on your
desk and asks one question:

> "Can you tell me what is happening?"

You stare at the screen. Where do you even begin?

Amina (that is you) takes a breath. Before analysing anything, there is a simpler
question to answer first.

::: {.think}
Sequencing machines are not perfect. They make mistakes.

So before you trust a single result, should you trust every read the machine gave you?
**Yes? No? Not sure?** Hold that thought. We will answer it together.
:::

## What even is a "read"?

Before we judge the data, we should know what it is. That 300 GB is not one long genome.
It is millions of short fragments, each read off the machine one at a time. Each fragment
is a **read**.

::: {.story}
Imagine marking thousands of handwritten exam papers. Some answers are neat and clear.
Some are an impossible scrawl.

A FASTQ file stores both things at once: **the answer** (the letters A, C, G, T) **and how
confident you are** in each letter. That confidence is the read's **quality**.
:::

A single read looks like this. Line 2 is the answer. Line 4 is the confidence, one symbol
per letter:

```text
@read_1
GATCTTAATGACTTTGTCTCTGATGCAGATTCAACTTTGATTGGTGATTGT
+
BIFDEHHFG?CDA@EF?@FAB@@D?E@BBA>@DAA@B@>?=?>;=><?@?<?
```

Higher symbols mean higher confidence. People talk about this as a **Q score**: Q30 means
the machine is 99.9% sure of that letter, Q20 means 99% sure. Quality usually starts high
and drops toward the end of a read. You will see that with your own eyes very soon.

## Short story, long story: two kinds of reads

::: {.insight}
Not all reads are the same size, and the difference is a real trade-off, not a "which is
better."
:::

![Short reads are many tiny fragments. Long reads are a few long ones covering the same genome. Each has strengths.](img/short-vs-long-reads.svg){width=820 fig-alt="Diagram comparing short reads and long reads over the same stretch of genome."}

- **Short reads** (Illumina, roughly 50 to 300 letters): cheap, extremely accurate per
  letter, and perfect for everyday work like counting and spotting single-letter changes.
  Their weakness is repeats, where short pieces are hard to place.
- **Long reads** (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore, tens of thousands of letters): they span
  repeats and big rearrangements, which is a superpower for assembly. Historically they
  traded away some per-letter accuracy, though that keeps improving.

For the rest of this story we work with short reads, the most common kind. (The tool we
use, FastQC, is built for them. Long reads use their own tools, like NanoPlot.)

## 💬 Why bother checking at all?

::: {.story}
Imagine buying tomatoes at the market. You do not throw them straight into the pot. You
look them over first. Any bruised? Rotten? Squished?

Quality control is exactly that. Before you cook with your data, you inspect it. A tool
called **FastQC** is your grocery inspection.
:::

So the answer to the question from the start is **No**. You do not blindly trust every
read. First you inspect. Then you decide. The blunt version:

> Garbage in, garbage out. Every result you ever produce is only as good as the reads it
> was built from.

## 🛠 Let's do it: inspect the reads

Now, and only now, the commands. You have your bench, your tools, and you can talk to
computers, so this will feel familiar. Install the tool once (using the Bioconda channel
from [Build Your Dry Lab Bench](../01-setup-environment/index.qmd)), then point it at your
reads:

```bash
conda create -n qc -c conda-forge -c bioconda fastqc fastp
conda activate qc
fastqc reads.fastq
```

FastQC thinks for a moment:

```text
Started analysis of reads.fastq
Approx 100% complete for reads.fastq
Analysis complete for reads.fastq
```

It writes a report (`reads_fastqc.html`). Open it. The single most useful plot is
**quality along the read**:

![Quality starts high (green zone) and slides into the red by the end of the read.](img/fastqc-raw-per-base-quality.png){width=620 fig-alt="FastQC per-base quality plot, declining along the read."}

Read it like a traffic light. **Green good, red bad.** Here the early letters are
excellent and the tail is poor. A gentle slope is normal. This one is steep.

Now look at **adapter content**:

![The adapter climbs to nearly half of the reads by the end. It should not be there.](img/fastqc-raw-adapter-content.png){width=620 fig-alt="FastQC adapter content plot rising toward the 3-prime end."}

That rising line is **adapter**, a bit of synthetic sequence that sneaks in when a fragment
is shorter than the read. It does not belong in your data.

## 🎉 What just happened?

::: {.insight}
Here is the part most people miss.

FastQC did **not** clean your data. It did not fix anything. It simply **described** it,
like a doctor reading an X-ray. It told you two things: the tail quality drops, and there
is adapter contamination.

Describing the problem is step one. Fixing it comes next.
:::

## 🧠 Think like a scientist, not a button

Before we start "fixing," a word that separates a button-pusher from a computational
biologist. **QC is not about chasing a wall of green ticks.** FastQC's pass, warn and fail
labels are rules of thumb tuned for a "typical" sample. They do not know what your
experiment is.

::: {.mistake}
The moment beginners see red, they panic and start deleting reads.

Do not. A red plot is information, not a verdict. Some "failures" are completely normal:
highly expressed genes look "over-duplicated" in RNA-seq, and that is fine. A GC warning
can just mean "this is the organism I study."
:::

Let your **next step** set your strictness:

- Calling single-letter variants? Be stricter. A wrong letter can become a false result.
- Counting genes for RNA-seq? More forgiving. A few noisy letters rarely change a count.
- Assembling a genome from scratch? Very sensitive to both errors and adapters.

For our data the honest read is simple: **two real problems**, adapter contamination and a
steep low-quality tail. Both worth fixing. That points to two decisions: remove adapters,
and trim the low-quality tail (a common cut-off is around Q20), while keeping reads long
enough to still be useful.

## 🛠 Let's do it: clean the reads

The tool **fastp** does both jobs at once. It finds adapters on its own, trims weak tails,
and writes its own report. This command encodes exactly the two decisions above:

```bash
fastp -i reads.fastq -o reads.trimmed.fastq \
      --cut_tail --cut_tail_mean_quality 20 \
      --length_required 30 \
      -h fastp.html
```

In plain words: trim the 3-prime tail once its quality drops below Q20, throw away any read
left shorter than 30 letters, and (automatically) strip adapters. Here is the **real
output**:

```text
Detecting adapter sequence for read1...
>Illumina TruSeq Adapter Read 1
AGATCGGAAGAGCACACGTCTGAACTCCAGTCA

Read1 before filtering:
Q20 bases: 70.32%

Read1 after filtering:
Q20 bases: 96.33%

reads with adapter trimmed: 5995
```

fastp **found the adapter by itself**, stripped it from 5,995 reads, and lifted the share
of high-confidence (Q20+) letters from **70% to 96%**. That is a real, measurable clean-up.

## 🎉 Did it actually work? Check again.

Never trust a fix you have not checked. Run FastQC on the cleaned reads and compare.

**Adapter content**, before and after:

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![Before: adapter climbs to nearly half.](img/fastqc-raw-adapter-content.png){fig-alt="Adapter content before trimming."}

![After: flat along the bottom. Gone.](img/fastqc-trimmed-adapter-content.png){fig-alt="Adapter content after trimming, essentially zero."}
:::

**Quality along the read**, before and after (notice the reads are now shorter, because
the worst tail letters were cut away):

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![Before: slides deep into the red.](img/fastqc-raw-per-base-quality.png){fig-alt="Per-base quality before trimming."}

![After: the worst tail is trimmed off.](img/fastqc-trimmed-per-base-quality.png){fig-alt="Per-base quality after trimming, shorter reads."}
:::

::: {.think}
Trimming did **not** turn every plot green, and that is fine. The reads are now different
lengths, so FastQC's "length" check will grumble. That grumble is expected and harmless.
What matters is the real win: adapters gone, and 96% of letters now high-confidence.

You interpret. You do not chase a perfect score.
:::

## 😂 Bioinformatics reality

::: {.reality}
Prof. Zola: "Is the data good?"<br>
Amina: "Define good."<br>
Prof. Zola: "..."<br>
Amina: "Exactly."
:::

## 🧩 Mini challenge

::: {.challenge}
Another team's per-base-quality plot sits comfortably in the **green** from the first
letter to the last, with no adapter showing.

Should you trim it? Think before you read on.

**Answer:** almost certainly not. If everything is green and clean, trimming would just
throw away good data for nothing. Fix real problems, not imaginary ones.
:::

## Three quick questions

Not graded. Just checking yourself.

1. Does FastQC **clean** your data, or **describe** it?
2. On the quality plot, is **red** good or bad?
3. True or false: after trimming, every FastQC plot should be green.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers
Describe it. Red is bad. False (some grumbles, like uneven read length, are expected after
trimming).
:::

## 🎯 Key takeaway

::: {.takeaway}
QC does not fix your data. It tells you whether you can trust it, and what to fix. Then you
clean the real problems, and check again. Judgment beats a perfect score.
:::

::: {.didyouknow}
FastQC is one of the most-run programs in all of biology. It has quietly inspected the data
behind an enormous share of published sequencing studies. For many results you have read
about, the very first thing anyone did to the data was exactly what you just did.
:::
